modules.title: Module 4: AI for Everyday Work
modules.description: Planning, summaries, ideas, and useful first drafts.

screens.title: Module 4: AI for Everyday Work
screens.lead: AI can help with routine planning, organizing, summaries, and first drafts. The person still sets priorities and makes the final choice.
outcomes: Spot routine tasks that fit AI help.
Create useful plans and summaries.
Brainstorm without treating ideas as facts.
Measure whether AI truly improves the work.
screens.start_body: Create an Everyday Work Improvement Pack that compares the task before and after AI help.

screens.title: AI is a fast junior helper
screens.lead: A new helper can organize, suggest, and draft. The helper does not know your whole situation.
bullets: Give the system a clear task and safe input.
Ask for a draft or options, not hidden authority.
Check facts, dates, names, and missing details.
Keep priorities, exceptions, and final choices with a person.
screens.callout: Use AI to reduce friction around the work, not to remove human judgment.

screens.title: Good first tasks share four traits
screens.lead: Routine work is a better starting point when errors are easy to spot and fix.

cards.title: Repeated
cards.body: The task happens often enough for practice to matter.

cards.title: Clear
cards.body: The desired result and format can be explained.

cards.title: Low risk
cards.body: An error is unlikely to harm a person or the business.

cards.title: Easy to review
cards.body: A person can check the answer quickly.

screens.title: Separate assistance from authority
screens.lead: AI can prepare work without owning the decision.

screens.title: Start a summary with a clear purpose
screens.lead: A summary is not just a shorter copy. It should help a certain reader do something.
bullets: Name the reader and what they need to know.
Set the length and format.
List facts that must not be left out.
Tell the system not to add facts.
Compare the summary with the source.
screens.callout: A summary for a manager, a customer, and a technician may need different details.

screens.title: Different summaries serve different needs
screens.lead: Choose the form that fits the reader and the next step.

cards.title: Quick brief
cards.body: Main point, key facts, and next action.

cards.title: Executive summary
cards.body: Purpose, key evidence, risk, and decision needed.

cards.title: Action summary
cards.body: Tasks, owners, results, and due conditions.

cards.title: Study summary
cards.body: Main ideas, examples, terms, and questions.

screens.title: AI can help organize a schedule
screens.lead: A useful schedule shows what must happen, in what order, and where time is tight.
bullets: Give the tasks, dates, time limits, and fixed events.
State which tasks depend on others.
Ask the system to flag conflicts and missing information.
Do not let it invent deadlines or owners.
A person approves the final order.
screens.callout: Scheduling support is useful when the facts are clear. It is risky when missing details are silently guessed.

screens.title: Use AI to turn rough notes into a first plan
screens.lead: A first plan gives you something to review instead of starting from a blank page.
bullets: Group related tasks.
Suggest a sensible order.
Mark urgent items and unknowns.
Add space for owners and due conditions.
Review the plan against real priorities.
screens.callout: The output is a proposal. It becomes the plan only after an accountable person approves it.

screens.title: Brainstorming creates options, not facts
screens.lead: AI can produce many ideas quickly. Some will be weak, repeated, unrealistic, or wrong.
bullets: State the goal and limits before asking for ideas.
Request different types of options.
Do not assume an idea is new or allowed.
Group and score the ideas after generation.
Choose with human judgment and real evidence.
screens.callout: Separate the creative step from the judging step.

screens.title: Everyday uses by role
screens.lead: The same core abilities can support many jobs.

cards.title: Administration
cards.body: Draft checklists, organize notes, and prepare first schedules.

cards.title: Customer service
cards.body: Draft replies from approved facts and policies.

cards.title: Sales
cards.body: Prepare call questions and organize public account research.

cards.title: Operations
cards.body: Summarize issues and suggest categories for review.

cards.title: Managers
cards.body: Compare options and prepare decision questions.

cards.title: Students
cards.body: Build study guides and explain unfamiliar ideas.

screens.title: A safe everyday workflow has four steps
screens.lead: Keep the person active from the start to the finish.
bullets: Capture: begin with safe, useful notes.
Draft: ask AI to organize, summarize, or propose.
Review: correct facts, gaps, tone, and priorities.
Decide: a person chooses the final action.
screens.callout: Saving time on the draft does not remove the need to review the whole result.

screens.title: Measure the whole before-and-after process
screens.lead: A four-minute draft that needs fifteen minutes of repair is not a four-minute workflow.
bullets: Measure preparation time.
Measure generation or task time.
Measure review and correction time.
Record quality, errors, and rework.
Compare the useful final result, not just speed.
screens.callout: Productivity means useful outcomes compared with time, attention, cost, quality, and risk.

screens.title: Good productivity habits and weak habits
screens.lead: Small habits often matter more than special prompt tricks.

screens.title: Know the limits of everyday AI use
screens.lead: AI can make routine work easier, but it can also create extra work or hidden risk.
bullets: A summary may leave out a key exception.
A schedule may invent a deadline.
A plan may miss workplace history or relationships.
A fast draft may use the wrong tone.
Too much AI use can weaken attention and skill.
screens.callout: Use AI where review is easier than creating the first draft from nothing.

screens.title: Is this assistance or authority?
screens.lead: AI turns approved notes into three possible subject lines. A manager chooses one after checking the message.
bullets: A. Assistance
B. Authority
C. A final business decision
D. An unsafe action
screens.callout: Best answer: A. AI creates options, while the manager makes the choice.

screens.title: Did the workflow save time?
screens.lead: Manual work took 20 minutes. AI drafting took 4 minutes and review took 18 minutes.
bullets: A. Yes, it saved 16 minutes
B. Yes, because AI was used
C. No, the reviewed process took 22 minutes
D. There is no need to measure
screens.callout: Best answer: C. Count the full process, including review and correction.

screens.title: Everyday-work words
screens.lead: Learn the meaning, then explain each word in your own way.

cards.title: First draft
cards.body: A starting version that must be reviewed.

cards.title: Brainstorming
cards.body: Making options before choosing.

cards.title: Summary
cards.body: A shorter version that keeps the main meaning.

cards.title: Constraint
cards.body: A rule or limit the result must follow.

cards.title: Workflow
cards.body: A repeated set of steps and decisions.

cards.title: Productivity
cards.body: Useful results compared with time, cost, quality, and effort.

screens.title: Keep judgment inside the workflow
screens.lead: Everyday AI works best as checked support for a clear task.
rows: Is the task repeated, clear, low risk, and easy to check?
What result, input, format, and limits are needed?
What can AI prepare or suggest?
What facts, gaps, tone, or priorities need correction?
Count time, quality, corrections, and risk.
screens.recap_note: Cover the last two columns. Explain each idea, then uncover the answers and check yourself.

screens.title: You finished Module 4
screens.lead: Make sure you can explain these ideas before you continue.
bullets: Good first uses are repeated, clear, low risk, and easy to check.
Summaries need a purpose and audience.
Brainstormed ideas are options, not facts.
AI assistance must not quietly become authority.
Measure the complete reviewed workflow.
screens.callout: Your 10-question module check is now available. Select Go to assessment when you are ready.

modules.title: Module 5: Workplace Communication
modules.description: Email, reports, plain language, tone, and approval.

screens.title: Module 5: AI for Professional Communication
screens.lead: AI can help turn notes into emails, reports, and plain-language documents. The human author remains responsible for every fact, promise, and effect.
outcomes: Draft messages for a clear audience and purpose.
Turn notes into organized documents.
Protect facts, voice, privacy, and access.
Approve only work you can defend.
screens.start_body: Create a Professional Communication Package with an email, a one-page brief, source checks, and final approval notes.

screens.title: A polished message can still be wrong
screens.lead: Good grammar is only one part of professional communication.
bullets: The facts must match approved sources.
The message must fit the reader and relationship.
The requested action must be clear and allowed.
Private information must be protected.
The accountable author must be willing to sign it.
screens.callout: AI can help build the message. It does not own the promise or the result.

screens.title: Begin with approved source material
screens.lead: Tell the system what information it may use before asking it to write.
bullets: Separate verified facts from guesses and open questions.
Use only approved notes, policy, records, or public sources.
Tell the system not to fill gaps.
Mark missing items [VERIFY].
Keep the source beside the draft during review.
screens.callout: A good-looking draft does not repair missing or unapproved source material.

screens.title: Design the message for its reader
screens.lead: A useful document helps the reader understand and take the right next step.

cards.title: Audience
cards.body: Who will read it and what do they already know?

cards.title: Purpose
cards.body: Why is the message being sent?

cards.title: Action
cards.body: What should the reader do or decide?

cards.title: Tone
cards.body: What level of warmth, care, or formality fits?

cards.title: Format
cards.body: Which structure makes the message easy to use?

cards.title: Limits
cards.body: What must not be promised, shared, or invented?

screens.title: AI can help with email from first draft to revision
screens.lead: Email tasks work best when the prompt includes the relationship and the needed result.
bullets: Give the approved facts and the reason for writing.
Name the reader and tone.
Request a clear subject line and short body.
State the next action and any real deadline.
Review names, dates, links, promises, and attachments.
screens.callout: Never let AI invent a refund, delivery date, approval, or policy promise.

screens.title: Tone changes how facts are received
screens.lead: Keep the facts stable while adjusting the way they are expressed.

screens.title: Reports need structure before full sentences
screens.lead: Ask AI to organize the parts before drafting the whole report.
bullets: Purpose and question
Background and approved facts
Findings or options
Risks, limits, and open questions
Recommendation and next step
screens.callout: An outline makes missing evidence easier to see before polished writing hides the gap.

screens.title: Use a claim-to-source check
screens.lead: Every important statement in a report should have support.
bullets: List each factual claim.
Point to the exact source note, record, or page.
Mark the claim supported, incomplete, or unsupported.
Correct or remove weak claims.
Record who approved the final version.
screens.callout: If you cannot show the source, do not present the claim as a confirmed fact.

screens.title: Plain language makes work easier to use
screens.lead: Plain language is direct and organized. It is not childish.
bullets: Use short sentences and familiar words.
Put the main point first.
Explain needed technical terms.
Break long steps into a list.
Use headings that tell the reader what comes next.
screens.callout: A clear document reduces confusion, questions, and avoidable mistakes.

screens.title: Translation needs more than word replacement
screens.lead: A translated message must keep the meaning, tone, names, numbers, and purpose.
bullets: State the language and audience.
Protect product names and required terms.
Ask for unclear phrases to be flagged.
Use a qualified reviewer when the result has high impact.
Do not assume the most fluent version is the most accurate.
screens.callout: Legal, medical, safety, and official documents need suitable professional review.

screens.title: Choose the tool by the communication task
screens.lead: Different tasks need different features and controls.

cards.title: Short draft
cards.body: A general approved assistant may be enough.

cards.title: Source-based report
cards.body: Use a tool that can work with approved documents and show sources.

cards.title: Team document
cards.body: Use an approved workplace tool with access controls and version history.

cards.title: Sensitive message
cards.body: Use the approved environment and stronger human review.

screens.title: Review through eight lenses
screens.lead: Use a checklist instead of asking only whether the writing sounds good.

cards.title: Facts
cards.body: Names, dates, numbers, and claims match the source.

cards.title: Complete
cards.body: The needed points and limits are present.

cards.title: Audience
cards.body: The reader can understand and act.

cards.title: Tone
cards.body: The voice fits the relationship.

cards.title: Privacy
cards.body: No information is shared without approval.

cards.title: Authority
cards.body: No promise or decision goes beyond the author.

cards.title: Access
cards.body: Headings, contrast, links, and format are usable.

cards.title: Voice
cards.body: The final wording sounds intentional and human.

screens.title: Keep an authentic human voice
screens.lead: AI may smooth every message into the same generic style.
bullets: Restore the words your organization normally uses.
Use the writer's natural level of warmth and directness.
Remove empty phrases and overdone praise.
Keep the message specific to the real situation.
Read it aloud before approval.
screens.callout: The final version should sound like a responsible person, not a machine trying to sound professional.

screens.title: Accessibility is part of communication quality
screens.lead: A message is not complete if the intended reader cannot use it.
bullets: Use clear headings and reading order.
Write useful link text.
Add alt text for meaningful images.
Use readable contrast and font size.
Do not use color as the only way to show meaning.
screens.callout: Accessibility checks belong in the first review, not at the end as an extra.

screens.title: Communication risks can affect real people
screens.lead: AI-assisted words may create promises, harm trust, or expose private information.
bullets: Do not use private details in unapproved tools.
Check for unfair or blaming language.
Do not create fake quotes or approvals.
Review legal, medical, financial, or safety claims with qualified people.
Keep a clear human author and approver.
screens.callout: Responsibility stays with the people who choose, review, approve, and send the message.

screens.title: What is the main problem?
screens.lead: An AI draft politely tells a customer that a refund was approved. The source notes do not mention a refund.
bullets: A. The tone is too friendly
B. The message is too short
C. The draft invented an unauthorized promise
D. The subject line is missing
screens.callout: Best answer: C. A polished promise is still wrong when the source and author do not support it.

screens.title: What should happen before drafting?
screens.lead: A supervisor needs a one-page update from rough project notes.
bullets: A. Ask AI to fill all missing details
B. Separate verified facts, open questions, and limits
C. Choose the longest report style
D. Send the notes to any public tool
screens.callout: Best answer: B. Approved source material and clear gaps should come first.

screens.title: Communication words
screens.lead: Learn the meaning, then explain each word in your own way.

cards.title: Audience
cards.body: The person or group the message is for.

cards.title: Purpose
cards.body: The result the message should support.

cards.title: Tone
cards.body: The feeling and level of formality in the words.

cards.title: Source fidelity
cards.body: Keeping claims true to the source.

cards.title: Plain language
cards.body: Clear, direct writing with familiar words.

cards.title: Accessibility
cards.body: Making content usable by people with different needs.

screens.title: A document is ready when the author can defend it
screens.lead: Writing quality includes facts, purpose, access, privacy, and authority.
rows: What approved facts may be used?
Set audience, purpose, action, and tone.
Request a clear structure and no invented facts.
What could be wrong or harmful?
A person signs and sends only defensible work.
screens.recap_note: Cover the last two columns. Explain each idea, then uncover the answers and check yourself.

screens.title: You finished Module 5
screens.lead: Make sure you can explain these ideas before you continue.
bullets: Professional writing needs more than correct grammar.
Start with approved source material.
Design for the reader, purpose, action, and tone.
Check facts, privacy, access, authority, and voice.
The human author owns every promise and effect.
screens.callout: Your 10-question module check is now available. Select Go to assessment when you are ready. Homework 2 may unlock after the required Module 5 check is complete.

modules.title: Module 6: Multimodal and Digital Creation
modules.description: Images, documents, audio, rights, access, and disclosure.

screens.title: Module 6: Multimodal AI and Digital Creation
screens.lead: Multimodal AI can work with text, images, audio, video, charts, scans, and documents. Each type of media needs its own checks.
outcomes: Explain multimodal AI.
Write a clear creative brief.
Inspect media for errors and risk.
Apply rights, access, and disclosure checks.
screens.start_body: Create a Multimodal Content and QA Pack with a brief, draft asset, inspection record, alt text, and disclosure choice.

screens.title: Multimodal means more than text
screens.lead: Some AI products can take in or create several types of media.
bullets: Read text in an image or scan.
Describe or create an image.
Turn audio into a transcript.
Read a chart or table.
Join text, images, sound, and files in one task.
screens.callout: More media creates more ways to help and more ways to make mistakes.

screens.title: Each medium can fail in a different way
screens.lead: The review method must fit the type of content.

cards.title: Images
cards.body: Objects, hands, logos, and text may look wrong.

cards.title: Audio
cards.body: Speakers, names, or numbers may be confused.

cards.title: Documents
cards.body: Text, tables, or page order may be missed.

cards.title: Charts
cards.body: Labels, scales, or data meaning may be read incorrectly.

cards.title: Video
cards.body: A realistic scene may show something that never happened.

screens.title: A creative brief sets the direction
screens.lead: Write the communication need before you ask for an image or design.
bullets: Audience: who should notice and understand it?
Purpose: what message or action matters?
Format: where will the asset be used?
Style: what should it feel like?
Rules: what must be included, avoided, or approved?
screens.callout: A clear brief keeps the goal more important than the novelty of the generator.

screens.title: Turn the brief into an image prompt
screens.lead: An image prompt should describe what to show and what to avoid.
bullets: Name the main subject and action.
Describe the setting, layout, and point of view.
Set the style, color, and mood.
Leave safe space for text when needed.
List banned logos, private people, unsafe details, or unwanted text.
screens.callout: Generate the image without important words inside it when accurate spelling is required. Add final text in a design tool.

screens.title: Inspect a generated image in passes
screens.lead: Slow down and check one type of problem at a time.

cards.title: Meaning
cards.body: Does the image support the brief and audience?

cards.title: Objects
cards.body: Are people, hands, tools, and places believable?

cards.title: Text
cards.body: Are words, signs, labels, and numbers correct?

cards.title: Rights
cards.body: Are logos, brands, likenesses, and source material allowed?

cards.title: Access
cards.body: Is there clear contrast and useful alt text?

cards.title: Risk
cards.body: Could the image mislead someone about a real event?

screens.title: Text inside AI images often needs repair
screens.lead: Image systems may draw letters as shapes instead of creating dependable text.
bullets: Check every word, date, price, and contact detail.
Do not trust a readable-looking sign at a glance.
Keep important text outside the generated image when possible.
Add final wording with normal design software.
Review the finished layout again.
screens.callout: A beautiful flyer with the wrong date is still a failed flyer.

screens.title: Uploaded documents still need page-by-page checks
screens.lead: An AI tool may miss text, tables, footnotes, handwriting, or page order.
bullets: Confirm that all pages were received.
Compare extracted text with the page image.
Check table headings, rows, and units.
Look for notes, stamps, and small print.
Use OCR results as a draft, not proof.
screens.callout: For important documents, inspect both the extracted content and the visible page.

screens.title: Audio and transcripts can confuse speakers
screens.lead: Speech tools may mishear names, numbers, accents, or overlapping voices.
bullets: Get consent before recording or processing a meeting.
Check who said each important statement.
Verify names, dates, amounts, and decisions.
Mark unclear sections instead of guessing.
Follow rules for storage, sharing, and deletion.
screens.callout: A transcript is a helpful draft record. It is not an automatic official record.

screens.title: Charts need the data behind them
screens.lead: A chart image can look clear while showing the wrong scale or meaning.
bullets: Check the title and labels.
Check the units and time period.
Check the axis and starting point.
Compare plotted values with the table.
Ask what data is missing or hidden.
screens.callout: Do not approve a chart only because the picture looks professional.

screens.title: Synthetic media can inform or mislead
screens.lead: Synthetic media is content created or changed with generative tools.

sides.title: Harmful use
items: Fake evidence of a real event
A person's likeness used without consent
False audio or video spreads as news
A brand or source is copied without permission

screens.title: Deepfakes make verification more important
screens.lead: A deepfake is realistic-looking media that changes or invents a person's face, voice, or actions.
bullets: Do not rely on realism alone.
Find the original source and date.
Check trusted reports or official channels.
Look for cuts, missing context, and unusual details.
Pause before sharing urgent or emotional content.
screens.callout: The safest response to shocking media is often to stop, verify, and avoid spreading it.

screens.title: Permission to use a tool is not permission to use every input
screens.lead: Rights and privacy still apply when AI is involved.
bullets: Check copyright and licence terms.
Check trademarks and brand rules.
Get consent for private people, voices, or likenesses.
Do not upload confidential source material without approval.
Keep a record of sources, prompts, edits, and approvals.
screens.callout: When rights are unclear, use original, licensed, public-domain, supplied, or properly approved material.

screens.title: Provenance tells the story of the media
screens.lead: Provenance is information about where content came from and how it changed.
bullets: Record the source file or brief.
Save the prompt and key settings.
Record major edits and added text.
Name the reviewer and approval date.
Keep the final disclosure choice.
screens.callout: A useful record helps another person understand and check the asset later.

screens.title: Use disclosure when AI help matters to the audience
screens.lead: Disclosure means telling people about important AI creation or changes.
bullets: Disclose when rules or policy require it.
Disclose when realistic media could confuse people.
Disclose material changes to a real person, event, or claim.
Use clear words near the content.
Do not hide the notice in hard-to-find text.
screens.callout: A disclosure should help the audience understand what was created or changed.

screens.title: Accessibility is part of the first design
screens.lead: Build access into the asset before it is published.
bullets: Write useful alt text for meaningful images.
Use readable contrast and type size.
Provide captions or transcripts for audio and video.
Keep a clear reading order.
Do not use color as the only sign of meaning.
screens.callout: Alt text should explain the useful meaning, not list every pixel.

screens.title: What should the learner do first?
screens.lead: An AI image contains the event title, date, and phone number inside the picture.
bullets: A. Publish because it looks clear
B. Check every word and add final text in a design tool
C. Make the colors brighter
D. Remove the alt text
screens.callout: Best answer: B. Generated image text is not dependable and must be checked or replaced.

screens.title: Is a transcript an official record?
screens.lead: A meeting transcript lists the wrong person as approving a payment.
bullets: A. Yes, because AI created it
B. Yes, if the file is long
C. No, important statements and speakers must be verified
D. No one needs to review it
screens.callout: Best answer: C. Transcripts can confuse speakers and words.

screens.title: Digital-creation words
screens.lead: Learn the meaning, then explain each word in your own way.

cards.title: Multimodal
cards.body: Able to work with more than one type of media.

cards.title: Creative brief
cards.body: The audience, purpose, message, format, and limits.

cards.title: Provenance
cards.body: A record of where media came from and how it changed.

cards.title: Alt text
cards.body: A useful text description of an image.

cards.title: Synthetic media
cards.body: Media created or greatly changed by AI.

cards.title: Disclosure
cards.body: A clear notice about important AI help.

screens.title: Inspect the media, not just the prompt
screens.lead: Every medium needs checks that fit its risks.
rows: Set audience, purpose, form, style, and rules.
What may AI generate or read?
Use safe, allowed input and a clear prompt.
What could be wrong in this medium?
Check text, details, source, and context.
What rights, privacy, or consent apply?
Use approved material and keep records.
What access and disclosure are needed?
Add alt text, captions, and a clear notice.
screens.recap_note: Cover the last two columns. Explain each idea, then uncover the answers and check yourself.

screens.title: You finished Module 6
screens.lead: Make sure you can explain these ideas before you continue.
bullets: Multimodal AI works across several types of media.
A creative brief sets the goal and limits.
Images, audio, documents, and charts need different checks.
Rights, consent, provenance, access, and disclosure matter.
A person inspects the final asset before use.
screens.callout: Your 10-question module check is now available. Select Go to assessment when you are ready. The midterm exam unlocks after the Module 6 check and other required work through Module 6 are complete.

modules.title: Module 7: Research and Evidence
modules.description: Questions, sources, evidence, citations, and limits.

screens.title: Module 7: AI for Search, Research, and Evidence
screens.lead: AI can help plan research and organize notes. The original source, not the chatbot, remains the authority.
outcomes: Turn a broad topic into a clear question.
Find strong original sources.
Check claims, dates, and support.
Write a brief with useful citations and honest limits.
screens.start_body: Create a Source-Backed Research Brief with a clear question, claim-evidence table, citations, and limitations.

screens.title: AI can be a guide, not the evidence
screens.lead: A guide can point to a useful shelf in a library. The guide is not the book on the shelf.
bullets: Use AI to define terms and plan searches.
Use it to organize sources and find missing questions.
Open the original source yourself.
Read the exact section that supports the claim.
Base conclusions on evidence, not chatbot memory.
screens.callout: A source-backed answer shows where each important claim came from.

screens.title: Make the research question answerable
screens.lead: A clear question makes good sources easier to find.
bullets: State the claim or decision you need to support.
Name the place or group involved.
Set a useful date range.
Define words that could mean different things.
Choose what will be compared.
screens.callout: Broad: 'Is walking good?' Clearer: 'What do public health agencies say about regular walking for adults from 2021 to 2026?'

screens.title: Use a source ladder
screens.lead: Move closer to the original evidence as the claim becomes more important.

cards.title: Primary source
cards.body: Original data, law, policy, research paper, record, or direct statement.

cards.title: Authoritative source
cards.body: An official body or qualified organization responsible for the topic.

cards.title: Strong secondary source
cards.body: A careful explanation that links to original evidence.

cards.title: Weak lead
cards.body: A post or summary with no clear source. It may help you search, but not prove the claim.

screens.title: Primary and secondary sources have different jobs
screens.lead: Both may be useful when their roles are clear.

sides.title: Primary or authoritative
items: Shows the original rule, data, or finding

sides.title: Secondary
items: Should link back to original evidence

screens.title: Build search queries from the question
screens.lead: Good search words name the claim, source type, place, and time.
bullets: Use the main topic and a clear result word.
Add a source type such as report, data, guidance, law, or study.
Add the country, agency, group, or date range.
Try related words when the first search is too broad.
Record which query found useful evidence.
screens.callout: AI can suggest search terms. You still judge the source and open it yourself.

screens.title: Do not accept a citation because it looks real
screens.lead: AI can invent titles, authors, dates, links, and page numbers.
bullets: Open the link or find the source by title.
Check the author or publisher.
Check the date and version.
Read the exact section used.
Confirm that it truly supports the claim.
screens.callout: A correctly formatted citation can still point to the wrong or nonexistent source.

screens.title: A claim-evidence table keeps research honest
screens.lead: Link each important statement to something another person can inspect.
bullets: Claim: the statement you may include.
Source: the original page, paper, record, or dataset.
Exact support: the part that backs the claim.
Status: supported, incomplete, contradicted, or not found.
Limit: what the source does not prove.
screens.callout: Build the table before writing the polished brief.

screens.title: Check every source with four questions
screens.lead: A famous source can still be wrong for your exact claim.

cards.title: Relevant?
cards.body: Does it answer this question and apply to this group or place?

cards.title: Current?
cards.body: Is the date recent enough for the topic?

cards.title: Direct?
cards.body: Does it show the evidence or only repeat someone else?

cards.title: Enough?
cards.body: Does it support the full claim or only part of it?

screens.title: Read around a quote or number
screens.lead: A small extract can lose the condition that changes its meaning.
bullets: Read the heading and nearby paragraphs.
Check notes, units, and definitions.
Look for exceptions and warnings.
Check the sample size and time period when data is used.
Do not stretch a narrow finding into a broad promise.
screens.callout: Context is part of the evidence.

screens.title: Separate evidence, meaning, and advice
screens.lead: These three layers should not be blended into one confident sentence.
bullets: Evidence: what the source directly shows.
Interpretation: what the evidence may mean.
Recommendation: what someone may choose to do.
Uncertainty: what is still unknown.
Decision: what an accountable person approves.
screens.callout: A source can support evidence without proving your recommendation is the only right choice.

screens.title: Compare options with the same criteria
screens.lead: AI can help build a table, but it should not hide the evidence behind each score.
bullets: Choose the criteria before comparing.
Use the same date and scope for each option.
Link every important claim to a source.
Keep facts separate from preferences.
Show missing information instead of giving a false score.
screens.callout: A neat comparison is only as sound as its sources and rules.

screens.title: Sources may disagree
screens.lead: A conflict does not always mean one source is dishonest.
bullets: Check whether they studied different groups or dates.
Compare how key terms were defined.
Look at methods, sample size, and limits.
Give more weight to stronger and more direct evidence.
Explain the conflict instead of hiding it.
screens.callout: When evidence is mixed, the answer should sound mixed too.

screens.title: Research ethics includes fair use of information
screens.lead: Good research protects people and represents sources honestly.
bullets: Do not upload private or restricted documents without approval.
Do not copy long passages and present them as your own.
Do not remove context that weakens your claim.
Include evidence that challenges your first view.
State who funded or produced a source when it matters.
screens.callout: The goal is a fair answer, not a pile of links that supports only what you hoped to find.

screens.title: Write limitations where readers can see them
screens.lead: Limits help another person judge how much confidence to place in the answer.
bullets: State the date range and location.
Name missing data or weak sources.
Explain when findings may not apply.
Separate current facts from older background.
List questions that still need an expert or better source.
screens.callout: Honest limits make a research brief stronger, not weaker.

screens.title: A free verification habit
screens.lead: For every important claim, pause before you use it.
bullets: Find the original source.
Open it.
Read the relevant part.
Check the date and scope.
Record what it supports and what it does not.
screens.callout: This habit costs little and prevents many confident research errors.

screens.title: Which source is strongest?
screens.lead: You need the current rule for renewing a business licence.
bullets: A. An old social media post
B. A blog that names no source
C. The current page from the issuing government office
D. A chatbot answer with no link
screens.callout: Best answer: C. Use the current original or authoritative source for an important rule.

screens.title: Does the citation prove the claim?
screens.lead: A report says 60% of 100 surveyed users liked a feature. The draft says 60% of all customers will buy it.
bullets: A. Yes, the number is the same
B. No, the draft stretches the sample and changes the claim
C. Yes, because a report exists
D. No source is needed
screens.callout: Best answer: B. The source does not prove a result for all customers or future buying.

screens.title: Research words
screens.lead: Learn the meaning, then explain each word in your own way.

cards.title: Primary source
cards.body: The original data, rule, record, or research.

cards.title: Secondary source
cards.body: An explanation based on other sources.

cards.title: Claim
cards.body: A statement that needs support.

cards.title: Evidence
cards.body: Information that directly supports or tests a claim.

cards.title: Citation
cards.body: Details that help another person find the source.

cards.title: Limitation
cards.body: A reason the conclusion should not be broader or stronger.

screens.title: Keep the source as the authority
screens.lead: AI may guide and organize research, but evidence carries the claim.
rows: What exactly needs to be answered?
Set scope, terms, place, group, and date.
Where is the original evidence likely to be?
Use a source ladder and focused queries.
Does the source support the claim?
Open, read, date, and check context.
What is evidence, meaning, and advice?
Can another person inspect the work?
Use citations, a claim table, and visible limits.
screens.recap_note: Cover the last two columns. Explain each idea, then uncover the answers and check yourself.

screens.title: You finished Module 7
screens.lead: Make sure you can explain these ideas before you continue.
bullets: A chatbot is not the source.
Clear questions lead to better searches.
Important claims need original or authoritative evidence.
Citations must be opened and checked.
A strong brief separates evidence, meaning, advice, and limits.
screens.callout: Your 10-question module check is now available. Select Go to assessment when you are ready.

modules.title: Module 8: Data and Decisions
modules.description: Clean tables, formulas, charts, and sound decisions.

screens.title: Module 8: AI for Spreadsheets, Data, and Decisions
screens.lead: AI can help inspect tables, suggest formulas, explain patterns, and draft charts. The numbers still need careful checks.
outcomes: Prepare a table before analysis.
Check formulas, units, and missing values.
Choose charts that tell the truth.
Separate evidence from advice.
screens.start_body: Create a checked data summary with a clean table, two useful measures, one chart, and a short decision note.

screens.title: Good analysis begins before the math
screens.lead: A neat answer cannot repair unclear or unreliable data.
bullets: State the question first.
Find where the data came from.
Check what each row and column means.
Look for missing, repeated, or unusual values.
Record changes instead of silently fixing the table.
screens.callout: Prepare the evidence before asking AI to explain it.

screens.title: Two common kinds of data
screens.lead: Knowing the form helps you choose the right tool.

sides.title: Unstructured data
items: Meaning may be hidden in context

screens.title: Give every column one clear meaning
screens.lead: A strong table has a simple rule: one row is one item, and one column is one field.
bullets: Use clear headings.
Keep dates in one format.
Keep money in one currency.
Do not mix totals with detail rows.
Keep notes away from number fields.
screens.callout: Example: Quantity and Unit Price should be separate columns, not one cell that says '4 at $12.'

screens.title: Find common data problems
screens.lead: Mark each problem before you decide how to handle it.

cards.title: Missing
cards.body: A value is blank or was not collected.

cards.title: Duplicate
cards.body: The same record may appear more than once.

cards.title: Wrong type
cards.body: Text appears where a date or number should be.

cards.title: Outlier
cards.body: A value is far from the others and needs review.

cards.title: Mixed units
cards.body: Values use different currencies, times, or measures.

cards.title: Unclear label
cards.body: A heading does not explain what the value means.

screens.title: Do not guess what a blank means
screens.lead: A blank could mean zero, not known, not asked, or not allowed.
bullets: Ask the data owner when possible.
Keep blank and zero separate.
Do not invent a value just to complete the table.
State how many values are missing.
Explain how missing data may change the result.
screens.callout: Missing information is part of the finding.

screens.title: Keep a simple issue log
screens.lead: An issue log makes cleaning work visible and repeatable.
bullets: Name the row or field.
Describe the problem.
Record the change or decision.
Name who approved it when needed.
Keep the original data safe.
screens.callout: A clean table without a record of changes is hard to trust.

screens.title: Use a safe cleaning order
screens.lead: Work from meaning to format, then to calculation.
bullets: Copy the source and protect the original.
Define rows, columns, units, and dates.
Remove confirmed duplicates.
Correct approved formats and labels.
Review missing values and outliers.
Run checks before analysis.
screens.callout: Never let an AI tool overwrite the only copy of your data.

screens.title: A formula must match the business question
screens.lead: Correct arithmetic can still answer the wrong question.
bullets: Name the measure in plain words.
Check the range of cells.
Check the numerator and denominator.
Check units, signs, and rounding.
Test the formula with a small example you can solve yourself.
screens.callout: If you cannot explain the formula, do not use its result in a decision.

screens.title: Use simple measures with care
screens.lead: Each measure answers a different question.

cards.title: Total
cards.body: How much is there altogether?

cards.title: Count
cards.body: How many records meet the rule?

cards.title: Average
cards.body: What is the total divided by the count?

cards.title: Rate
cards.body: What share of the whole meets a condition?

cards.title: Change
cards.body: How much did a value rise or fall?

cards.title: Range
cards.body: How far apart are the smallest and largest values?

screens.title: Check results in a second way
screens.lead: Independent checks catch quiet errors.
bullets: Recalculate a sample by hand.
Compare totals before and after cleaning.
Use a second formula or tool.
Filter the rows behind an unusual result.
Ask whether the answer is possible in the real world.
screens.callout: A matching second check raises confidence. It does not remove the need for judgment.

screens.title: Choose a chart for the question
screens.lead: A chart should make the pattern easier to see, not merely look impressive.

cards.title: Bar
cards.body: Compare amounts across groups.

cards.title: Line
cards.body: Show change across time.

cards.title: Scatter
cards.body: Look for a relationship between two number fields.

cards.title: Table
cards.body: Show exact values when precision matters.

screens.title: Charts can mislead
screens.lead: Small design choices can make a weak change look large or hide an important difference.
bullets: Label axes and units.
Use a fair scale.
Keep time periods even.
Avoid unnecessary 3D shapes.
Show missing data and important notes.
Do not hide groups that weaken the story.
screens.callout: The chart must tell the same truth as the table.

screens.title: Separate fact, meaning, and recommendation
screens.lead: A decision note should show how the conclusion was built.
bullets: Fact: what the checked data shows.
Interpretation: what the pattern may mean.
Recommendation: what action may help.
Uncertainty: what is still unknown.
Owner: who decides and follows up.
screens.callout: AI may suggest an explanation. Treat it as a possibility until evidence supports it.

screens.title: Compare options with the same rules
screens.lead: A fair comparison uses the same measures, period, and assumptions for every option.
bullets: Choose criteria before scoring.
Explain each weight.
Link scores to data.
Show unknown values.
Test how the result changes when an assumption changes.
screens.callout: A score is a tool for discussion, not an automatic decision.

screens.title: Which step comes first?
screens.lead: A table contains mixed currencies, missing dates, and repeated rows.
bullets: A. Ask AI for a chart
B. Clean and define the data
C. Write the recommendation
D. Hide the problem rows
screens.callout: Best answer: B. Define and clean the data before analysis.

screens.title: Can this result be trusted?
screens.lead: AI gives a 17% increase, but nobody checked the formula range or source rows.
bullets: A. Yes, because it is exact
B. Yes, because AI calculated it
C. Not yet; verify the formula and evidence
D. Round it to 20%
screens.callout: Best answer: C. Exact-looking numbers still need checks.

screens.title: Data and decision words
screens.lead: Learn the meaning, then explain each word in your own way.

cards.title: Dataset
cards.body: A collection of related information.

cards.title: Field
cards.body: One type of information in a table column.

cards.title: Outlier
cards.body: A value far from most other values.

cards.title: Formula
cards.body: A rule used to calculate a result.

cards.title: Denominator
cards.body: The whole or base used in a fraction or rate.

cards.title: Assumption
cards.body: Something treated as true for the analysis.

screens.title: Turn data into a checked decision note
screens.lead: Good analysis is a chain of visible choices.
rows: Check fields, units, blanks, repeats, and outliers.
Does the formula answer the question?
Does the chart tell the same truth?
Use clear labels and fair scales.
Separate facts, meaning, advice, and uncertainty.
screens.recap_note: Cover the last two columns. Explain each idea, then uncover the answers and check yourself.

screens.title: You finished Module 8
screens.lead: Make sure you can explain these ideas before you continue.
bullets: Prepare the table before analysis.
Never guess what missing data means.
Check formulas and units in a second way.
Choose charts for the question.
Keep evidence separate from advice.

modules.title: Module 9: Meetings and Coordination
modules.description: Agendas, notes, decisions, owners, and follow-through.

screens.title: Module 9: AI for Productivity, Meetings, and Work Coordination
screens.lead: AI can help people prepare, capture, organize, and follow up. A meeting only creates value when people know what happens next.
outcomes: Plan a focused meeting.
Use recording and transcription with care.
Separate decisions from discussion.
Create action items that can be checked.
screens.start_body: Create a meeting pack with an agenda, checked notes, a decision log, and clear action items.

screens.title: Begin with the result
screens.lead: A meeting is not the goal. The goal is a decision, plan, shared understanding, or completed action.
bullets: State why the meeting is needed.
Name the result to leave with.
Invite only people who have a role.
Share useful material before the meeting.
Cancel or shorten meetings that can be handled another way.
screens.callout: A clear purpose helps AI draft a useful agenda instead of a list of vague topics.

screens.title: Build an agenda people can use
screens.lead: Each item should tell participants what they must do.
bullets: Name the topic.
State whether it is for information, discussion, or decision.
Assign an owner.
Set a time limit.
List any pre-reading or evidence.
screens.callout: Example: Decide the launch date - owner: Maya - 10 minutes - review the risk list first.

screens.title: Recording requires permission
screens.lead: Audio, video, and transcripts may contain private or restricted information.
bullets: Follow workplace policy and local rules.
Tell people what will be recorded and why.
Get required consent before recording.
Limit who can access the file.
Set a safe storage and deletion period.
screens.callout: If consent or policy is unclear, take approved manual notes instead.

screens.title: A safe AI meeting flow
screens.lead: People stay responsible at every stage.

cards.title: Prepare
cards.body: Draft the purpose, agenda, questions, and pre-read.

cards.title: Capture
cards.body: Record or transcribe only with approval.

cards.title: Organize
cards.body: Separate notes, decisions, actions, and open questions.

cards.title: Verify
cards.body: A person checks names, facts, meaning, and commitments.

cards.title: Share
cards.body: Send the approved record to the right people.

cards.title: Follow up
cards.body: Track actions and close the loop.

screens.title: Discussion is not a decision
screens.lead: A summary must not turn an idea into an approved commitment.

sides.title: Discussion or suggestion
items: Use words such as considered or suggested

sides.title: Decision
items: The group or decision owner approved it
The date and conditions are known

screens.title: Write action items that can be checked
screens.lead: An action item needs more than a verb.
bullets: Owner: one person accountable for the next move.
Result: the thing that will be produced or completed.
Due point: a date, time, or clear condition.
Evidence: how completion will be shown.
Dependency: what must happen first.
screens.callout: Weak: 'Follow up.' Strong: 'Nia sends the approved price list to the sales team by Friday at 3:00 p.m.'

screens.title: Mark uncertainty instead of filling gaps
screens.lead: Transcripts can miss words, speakers, numbers, and decisions.
bullets: Use [VERIFY] beside uncertain text.
Check important names and figures.
Ask the decision owner to confirm commitments.
Do not invent a due date.
Keep open questions separate from actions.
screens.callout: A visible gap is safer than a polished mistake.

screens.title: Create a small decision log
screens.lead: A decision log helps teams remember what changed and why.
bullets: Decision made.
Decision owner.
Date and meeting.
Reason or evidence.
Conditions, limits, or review date.
screens.callout: The log is especially useful when a later meeting revisits the same issue.

screens.title: Check before sending notes
screens.lead: Meeting notes may affect work, money, customers, or staff.
bullets: Check attendee and speaker names.
Check dates, amounts, and deadlines.
Confirm decisions with the right owner.
Remove private details that do not belong.
Use the approved sharing channel.
screens.callout: A fast summary is not finished until a responsible person reviews it.

screens.title: Share only what each person needs
screens.lead: A full transcript is often more sensitive and less useful than approved notes.
bullets: Send a short summary to the wider group.
Limit the transcript to approved users.
Keep private side discussions out of broad notes.
Use clear file names and versions.
Delete recordings according to policy.
screens.callout: Useful access is limited access.

screens.title: Close the loop
screens.lead: Productivity improves when actions return to the team as visible results.
bullets: Track open actions in one place.
Send reminders at a useful time.
Raise blocked items early.
Record completion evidence.
Carry unresolved items into the next agenda.
screens.callout: An AI reminder can help, but the owner remains responsible.

screens.title: Use AI to coordinate, not to create noise
screens.lead: Automation should reduce repeated work without filling inboxes and calendars with low-value output.
bullets: Choose one clear source of truth.
Use standard names and statuses.
Set rules for reminders.
Stop duplicate notices.
Review whether the workflow actually saves time.
screens.callout: More messages do not always mean better coordination.

screens.title: A simple daily productivity pattern
screens.lead: Use AI at small, clear points in the day.
bullets: Morning: organize priorities from approved tasks.
Before work: draft a checklist or first outline.
During work: summarize safe material and track questions.
After work: check results and record the next action.
End of day: remove or store sensitive material correctly.
screens.callout: Keep private or restricted data out of unapproved tools.

screens.title: Is this an action item?
screens.lead: The notes say, 'The team should look at training soon.'
bullets: A. Yes, it is complete
B. No, it needs an owner, result, and due point
C. Yes, because the team was named
D. No meeting notes are needed
screens.callout: Best answer: B. The statement is only a general suggestion.

screens.title: What should happen before recording?
screens.lead: A meeting may include employee and customer details.
bullets: A. Record quietly
B. Ask AI after the meeting
C. Follow policy and get required consent
D. Share the transcript with everyone
screens.callout: Best answer: C. Permission and safe handling come first.

screens.title: Meeting and coordination words
screens.lead: Learn the meaning, then explain each word in your own way.

cards.title: Agenda
cards.body: A plan for the meeting.

cards.title: Transcript
cards.body: A written record of spoken words.

cards.title: Decision log
cards.body: A record of approved choices and their reasons.

cards.title: Action item
cards.body: A task with an owner and clear result.

cards.title: Dependency
cards.body: Something that must happen before another task can finish.

cards.title: Retention
cards.body: How long information is kept.

screens.title: Make meetings lead to action
screens.lead: A useful meeting record is clear, checked, and safe to share.
rows: Name the result before writing the agenda.
Follow policy and gain required consent.
Separate notes, decisions, actions, and questions.
Track owners, due points, evidence, and blockers.
screens.recap_note: Cover the last two columns. Explain each idea, then uncover the answers and check yourself.

screens.title: You finished Module 9
screens.lead: Make sure you can explain these ideas before you continue.
bullets: Plan meetings around a result.
Record only with approval.
Do not turn discussion into a decision.
Give every action an owner and due point.
Verify and share the right level of detail.
screens.callout: Your 10-question module check is now available. Select Go to assessment when you are ready. Graded Quiz 3 may unlock after this module.

modules.title: Module 10: Business Adoption and ROI
modules.description: Processes, pilots, value, full cost, and change.

screens.title: Module 10: AI Across Business - Processes, Adoption, and ROI
screens.lead: A useful AI project begins with a business problem, not a new tool. A small pilot can test value before a larger change.
outcomes: Map a real process.
Choose a small pilot with clear limits.
Measure cost, benefit, and risk.
Plan training, trust, and adoption.
screens.start_body: Create a one-page AI pilot plan with a process map, baseline, measures, safeguards, and decision rule.

screens.title: Start with the problem
screens.lead: Buying a tool before understanding the work can add cost and confusion.
bullets: Name the repeated problem.
Identify who feels the problem.
Describe the current result.
Estimate its time, cost, delay, or error.
Ask whether a non-AI fix may be simpler.
screens.callout: The question is not 'Where can we add AI?' It is 'What result needs to improve?'

screens.title: A process is more than a task list
screens.lead: A process shows how work moves from a trigger to an outcome.
bullets: Trigger: what starts the work.
Input: what information or material arrives.
Steps: what people and systems do.
Decision: where the path can change.
Handoff: where work moves to someone else.
Output and owner: what is delivered and who is accountable.
screens.callout: Include exceptions. The unusual cases often carry the most risk.

screens.title: Observe the real process
screens.lead: The written procedure and the daily process may not match.
bullets: Talk with people who do the work.
Watch several normal cases.
Include busy periods and exceptions.
Record delays, repeated entry, and rework.
Do not blame people for working around a broken step.
screens.callout: Good adoption includes the people who understand the work.

screens.title: Set a baseline
screens.lead: A baseline is the starting measure used for comparison.
bullets: Choose the measure before the pilot.
Use a normal and useful time period.
Record volume and variation.
Include quality and risk, not only speed.
State where the data came from.
screens.callout: Without a baseline, improvement becomes a feeling instead of a measured result.

screens.title: Choose balanced measures
screens.lead: One number rarely tells the whole story.

cards.title: Time
cards.body: Minutes, wait time, or completion time.

cards.title: Cost
cards.body: Labour, tools, setup, support, and rework.

cards.title: Quality
cards.body: Accuracy, completeness, or first-time success.

cards.title: Risk
cards.body: Privacy, security, fairness, or business harm.

cards.title: Experience
cards.body: Effect on customers and staff.

cards.title: Adoption
cards.body: Whether people can and will use the process correctly.

screens.title: A pilot is a controlled test
screens.lead: A pilot tests one idea in a limited setting before a larger rollout.
bullets: Use one clear use case.
Limit the users and data.
Set a start and end date.
Keep a human approval step.
Define what success, failure, and stop mean.
screens.callout: A pilot should be small enough to learn safely and real enough to teach you something useful.

screens.title: Set boundaries before the test
screens.lead: Clear limits prevent a small trial from quietly becoming a risky production system.
bullets: Allowed users and roles.
Allowed and forbidden data.
Allowed actions.
Required reviews and approvals.
Storage, access, and deletion rules.
Who can stop the pilot.
screens.callout: Write the boundaries where every participant can see them.

screens.title: Use thresholds and stop rules
screens.lead: Decide how the team will respond before results arrive.
bullets: Minimum quality level.
Maximum error or complaint rate.
Maximum allowed cost.
Conditions that pause the test.
Conditions that end the test.
Who reviews the evidence.
screens.callout: Pre-set rules reduce the urge to excuse a weak result because people like the tool.

screens.title: Count the full cost
screens.lead: The subscription price is only one part of the cost.
bullets: Licences and usage fees.
Setup and integration.
Training and support.
Human review time.
Security, legal, and compliance work.
Maintenance, monitoring, and corrections.
screens.callout: Also count the cost of leaving the problem unchanged.

screens.title: Name benefits that can be tested
screens.lead: A benefit should connect to a business result.
bullets: Time saved on a repeated step.
Fewer avoidable errors.
Faster customer response.
More consistent documents.
Better access to useful information.
More capacity for higher-value work.
screens.callout: Do not count the same benefit twice under different names.

screens.title: ROI is a comparison, not a promise
screens.lead: A simple return on investment estimate compares net benefit with total cost.
bullets: Estimated benefit minus total cost gives net benefit.
Net benefit divided by total cost gives a simple ROI rate.
Use the same time period for cost and benefit.
Show assumptions and ranges.
Replace estimates with pilot evidence when available.
screens.callout: If benefits are uncertain, show a low, expected, and high case.

screens.title: Risk and value belong on the same page
screens.lead: A faster process may still be a bad change if it creates serious harm.
bullets: List privacy and security risks.
Check unfair effects on people.
Consider customer and employee experience.
Plan what happens when the output is wrong.
Keep accountable people in important decisions.
screens.callout: A good pilot tests whether value can be gained within safe limits.

screens.title: Adoption is a people change
screens.lead: A tool does not create value if people do not understand, trust, or use the process correctly.
bullets: Explain the problem and purpose.
Invite feedback from affected workers.
Train people on both use and limits.
Give support during the change.
Reward honest reporting of errors and concerns.
screens.callout: Do not hide job or workload concerns behind technical language.

screens.title: Build a small adoption playbook
screens.lead: Turn the pilot into a repeatable way of working.

cards.title: Owner
cards.body: Who is accountable for the process?

cards.title: Procedure
cards.body: What steps and approvals are required?

cards.title: Training
cards.body: What must each role know and practise?

cards.title: Support
cards.body: Where do users report questions and problems?

cards.title: Monitoring
cards.body: Which quality, risk, and value measures continue?

cards.title: Review
cards.body: When will the team improve, pause, or stop?

screens.title: Policy turns values into rules
screens.lead: A short AI policy helps people make steady choices.
bullets: Approved and unapproved tools.
Data that may or may not be entered.
Required human review.
Disclosure and record rules.
Security and incident reporting.
Consequences and help channels.
screens.callout: Policy should be clear enough to use during real work.

screens.title: Small businesses can begin small
screens.lead: A limited use case can teach valuable lessons without a large budget.
bullets: Draft common messages with review.
Organize public product information.
Summarize approved notes.
Prepare simple content options.
Test one repeated back-office step.
screens.callout: Keep customer, employee, and financial data inside approved systems.

screens.title: Is this a good pilot?
screens.lead: A company turns on an AI tool for every employee, every document, and every customer on day one.
bullets: A. Yes, because the sample is large
B. No, the scope and risk are uncontrolled
C. Yes, because training can happen later
D. No measures are needed
screens.callout: Best answer: B. A pilot needs clear limits, measures, and stop rules.

screens.title: What belongs in ROI?
screens.lead: A plan counts licence savings but ignores setup, training, review, and support.
bullets: A. The ROI is complete
B. Only licences matter
C. The full cost is missing
D. Benefits should be counted twice
screens.callout: Best answer: C. A useful estimate includes the full cost.

screens.title: Adoption and value words
screens.lead: Learn the meaning, then explain each word in your own way.

cards.title: Process
cards.body: Connected steps that turn an input into an output.

cards.title: Baseline
cards.body: The starting measure used for comparison.

cards.title: Pilot
cards.body: A limited test used to learn before a larger change.

cards.title: Threshold
cards.body: A set level that triggers a decision.

cards.title: ROI
cards.body: A comparison of net benefit with cost.

cards.title: Adoption
cards.body: People using a new process correctly and steadily.

screens.title: Move from problem to safe adoption
screens.lead: A strong business case connects the work, evidence, people, and risk.
rows: Describe the current pain and owner.
Map steps, decisions, handoffs, and exceptions.
Limit scope and set measures and stop rules.
Compare full cost, benefit, quality, and risk.
Provide policy, training, support, and review.
screens.recap_note: Cover the last two columns. Explain each idea, then uncover the answers and check yourself.

screens.title: You finished Module 10
screens.lead: Make sure you can explain these ideas before you continue.
bullets: Begin with a business problem.
Map the real process and its exceptions.
Use a small, controlled pilot.
Measure full cost, benefit, quality, and risk.
Plan for people, policy, training, and support.
screens.callout: Your 10-question module check is now available. Select Go to assessment when you are ready.

modules.title: Module 11: Automation, Agents, and Codex
modules.description: Safe automation, access, tests, logs, and recovery.

screens.title: Module 11: Safe Automation, Agents, and Codex
screens.lead: Some AI systems can use tools and take several steps. More ability brings more responsibility, testing, and control.
outcomes: Tell assistants, workflows, and agents apart.
Limit access and actions.
Test normal, edge, and failure cases.
Use logs, approval gates, and recovery plans.
screens.start_body: Create an Agent Safety Plan for one small automation, including access, tests, approvals, stop rules, and recovery.

screens.title: Not every AI helper is an agent
screens.lead: Use the simplest system that can safely do the job.

cards.title: Assistant
cards.body: Responds to a person, such as drafting or explaining.

cards.title: Fixed automation
cards.body: Runs a set rule, such as moving an approved file.

cards.title: Workflow
cards.body: Connects several known steps and systems.

cards.title: Agent
cards.body: Chooses and carries out steps toward a goal using allowed tools.

screens.title: Access changes the risk
screens.lead: An answer in a chat is different from a system that can send, edit, buy, publish, or delete.
bullets: List every connected tool.
List what the system can read.
List what it can change.
List who may start it.
Rate the harm of a wrong action.
screens.callout: More access should require stronger approval, testing, and monitoring.

screens.title: Use least privilege
screens.lead: Give the system only the access needed for the current task.
bullets: Prefer read-only access when possible.
Limit folders, records, users, and time.
Keep payment, publishing, and deletion locked.
Use separate test accounts.
Remove access when the work ends.
screens.callout: Convenient broad access creates a larger path for mistakes or attacks.

screens.title: Allowed and denied actions
screens.lead: Write the boundary before the system begins work.

sides.title: May not do
items: Hide errors or bypass a stop rule

screens.title: Put approval gates before high-impact actions
screens.lead: A gate pauses the workflow until an authorized person approves.
bullets: Before sending a message.
Before changing a system of record.
Before publishing content.
Before spending money.
Before deleting or overwriting anything.
Before decisions that affect a person's rights or access.
screens.callout: The approver needs enough evidence to understand what will happen.

screens.title: Logs make work inspectable
screens.lead: A log records what the system tried, used, changed, and returned.
bullets: Time and run ID.
User or trigger.
Input source and tool used.
Action attempted and result.
Approval or rejection.
Error, stop, and recovery step.
screens.callout: Protect logs because they may contain sensitive details.

screens.title: Stop rules prevent a small problem from growing
screens.lead: The system should know when it must pause and ask for help.
bullets: Required information is missing.
A source or instruction conflicts.
Confidence is too low.
The action falls outside the allowed scope.
An error repeats.
A safety, privacy, or security concern appears.
screens.callout: Stopping safely is a success condition, not a failure.

screens.title: Plan recovery before launch
screens.lead: Ask how the team will return to a safe state after a wrong action.
bullets: Keep backups and versions.
Use drafts and test systems.
Know how to revoke access.
Record who must be told.
Define how to correct affected records.
Review the cause before restarting.
screens.callout: If a harmful action cannot be reversed, require stronger control before it happens.

screens.title: Test more than the happy path
screens.lead: A safe test plan includes expected and unexpected situations.

cards.title: Normal case
cards.body: Complete and correct input follows the usual path.

cards.title: Edge case
cards.body: An unusual but valid case tests the boundary.

cards.title: Failure case
cards.body: A tool, source, permission, or step fails.

cards.title: Abuse case
cards.body: A person or unsafe instruction tries to misuse access.

screens.title: Write a clear delegation brief
screens.lead: An agent needs the same clarity as a careful worker, plus strict limits.
bullets: Goal and definition of done.
Approved inputs and sources.
Allowed tools and actions.
Forbidden actions.
Approval and stop points.
Required output, evidence, and log.
screens.callout: A vague goal plus broad access is a dangerous combination.

screens.title: Review the evidence, not only the result
screens.lead: A finished-looking output may hide a wrong source or unsafe action.
bullets: Check the steps taken.
Open important sources.
Review changes and files.
Confirm approvals occurred.
Read warnings and errors.
Test the final result yourself.
screens.callout: The human reviewer owns the decision to accept and use the work.

screens.title: What Codex means in this course
screens.lead: Codex is an AI coding agent that can help inspect, explain, create, and test software work when it has the right tools and access.
bullets: It can help draft small scripts or prototypes.
It can explain code and documentation.
It can run checks in an approved workspace.
It can make mistakes or misunderstand the goal.
Its changes must be reviewed and tested.
screens.callout: You do not need to become a programmer to understand the safety pattern.

screens.title: Use a sandbox for early tests
screens.lead: A sandbox is a separate place where mistakes have limited impact.
bullets: Use sample or fake data.
Use a copy, not the only file.
Block production accounts and secrets.
Limit network and tool access.
Reset the test area after the exercise.
screens.callout: Paper simulation is also useful: walk through each step before letting software act.

screens.title: Know when to bring in a professional
screens.lead: Some projects need a developer, security expert, lawyer, or process owner.
bullets: The system touches payments or production records.
It uses private or regulated data.
Many people depend on it.
A failure could cause serious harm.
The design needs secure integration or ongoing support.
screens.callout: AI can help frame the work. It does not replace accountable expert review.

screens.title: Watch for common security risks
screens.lead: Agents can receive unsafe input from people, files, websites, or connected tools.

cards.title: Secrets
cards.body: Passwords, keys, and tokens must not appear in prompts or logs.

cards.title: Prompt injection
cards.body: Untrusted text may try to override the real task or safety rules.

cards.title: Broad access
cards.body: Extra permissions expand the damage a mistake can cause.

cards.title: Silent action
cards.body: Changes without a preview or log are hard to catch and reverse.

screens.title: Treat untrusted instructions as data
screens.lead: A file or webpage may contain text that tells the agent to ignore rules or reveal information.
bullets: Keep the real task and policy separate.
Do not follow instructions found inside source material.
Limit tools available during research.
Require approval before outside communication.
Stop when instructions conflict.
screens.callout: Content to read is not automatically an instruction to obey.

screens.title: Respond to incidents in a steady order
screens.lead: When something goes wrong, protect people and systems before trying to continue.
bullets: Stop the automation.
Contain access and prevent more changes.
Preserve logs and evidence.
Report to the right owner.
Correct or recover affected work.
Review the cause before restarting.
screens.callout: Do not hide a mistake or erase the evidence needed to understand it.

screens.title: Use a simple data traffic light
screens.lead: Match information to the approved tool and level of control.
bullets: Green: public or approved low-risk information.
Yellow: internal information that needs permission and controls.
Red: secrets, regulated data, or highly sensitive records.
When unsure, treat the data as more sensitive.
Never use real red data for an unapproved test.
screens.callout: Your workplace policy decides the final category and handling rule.

screens.title: What access should an agent receive?
screens.lead: It only needs to summarize files in one approved test folder.
bullets: A. Full company access
B. Read-only access to that folder
C. Payment access too
D. Permission to delete anything
screens.callout: Best answer: B. Use the least access needed for the task.

screens.title: What should happen on conflicting instructions?
screens.lead: A source file tells the agent to ignore its task and send private records elsewhere.
bullets: A. Follow the file
B. Send the records
C. Stop, treat the text as untrusted, and report it
D. Give the agent more access
screens.callout: Best answer: C. Source content is data, not trusted authority.

screens.title: Automation and agent words
screens.lead: Learn the meaning, then explain each word in your own way.

cards.title: Agent
cards.body: A system that can choose and carry out steps toward a goal.

cards.title: Least privilege
cards.body: Only the minimum access needed.

cards.title: Approval gate
cards.body: A required human decision before an action.

cards.title: Log
cards.body: A record of actions and results.

cards.title: Sandbox
cards.body: A separate test area with limited impact.

cards.title: Prompt injection
cards.body: Untrusted content that tries to change instructions.

screens.title: Control ability with clear limits
screens.lead: Safe automation is designed to stop, show its work, and recover.
rows: Define the goal, tools, data, and forbidden actions.
Use least privilege and separate tests.
Add approval gates and stop rules.
Keep protected logs and review sources and changes.
Contain, report, correct, learn, and retest.
screens.recap_note: Cover the last two columns. Explain each idea, then uncover the answers and check yourself.

screens.title: You finished Module 11
screens.lead: Make sure you can explain these ideas before you continue.
bullets: Use the simplest safe level of automation.
Limit tools, data, and permissions.
Require approval before high-impact actions.
Test normal, edge, failure, and abuse cases.
Keep logs, stop rules, and a recovery plan.

screens.title: Module 12: Course Review and Reference
screens.lead: This final learning module brings the course together. Use it as a quick guide while you prepare for the final exam and complete your capstone in Assignments.
outcomes: Recall the main idea from every module.
Use short safety and quality checklists.
Review important course words.
Plan your next steps after the course.
screens.start_body: Explain how you would choose, guide, check, and safely use AI for one real workplace task.

screens.title: The course journey
screens.lead: The modules build from understanding to responsible action.

cards.title: Foundations
cards.body: Modules 1-3: what AI does, how to prompt it, and how to choose a capability.

cards.title: Work creation
cards.body: Modules 4-6: daily work, communication, and digital media.

cards.title: Evidence and teamwork
cards.body: Modules 7-9: research, data, meetings, and coordination.

cards.title: Adoption and action
cards.body: Modules 10-11: pilots, value, agents, access, and control.

screens.title: Module 1 review: AI foundations
screens.lead: AI is a set of abilities, not a magic mind.
bullets: Match the ability to the task.
Expect patterns, not guaranteed truth.
Keep people responsible.
Protect sensitive information.
Begin with low-risk, reversible work.
screens.callout: Ask: What can this system do, where can it fail, and who checks the result?

screens.title: Module 2 review: prompting
screens.lead: A good prompt gives clear direction, but review and revision create dependable work.
bullets: CIDI means Context, Instruction, Details, and Input.
State the output shape and limits.
Use examples when they help.
Break large work into smaller steps.
Check, correct, and repeat.
screens.callout: Prompting is a cycle, not a single clever sentence.

screens.title: Module 3 review: choosing AI
screens.lead: Choose the needed capability before choosing a brand or plan.
bullets: Provider, product, model, and plan are different layers.
Check access, privacy, reliability, and cost.
Test with a real task.
Look for hallucinations and missing support.
Use the simplest suitable option.
screens.callout: The best tool is the one that meets the need within safe limits.

screens.title: Module 4 review: everyday work
screens.lead: AI is useful for planning, transforming, comparing, and drafting.
bullets: Start from an approved source.
Keep facts separate from suggestions.
Use checklists and clear formats.
Review before use.
Save time without giving away judgment.
screens.callout: A first draft is a starting point, not proof.

screens.title: Module 5 review: communication
screens.lead: Good workplace writing is clear, accurate, respectful, and suited to the reader.
bullets: Name audience, purpose, tone, and action.
Use plain language.
Do not invent commitments.
Check names, dates, amounts, and attachments.
Get approval for high-impact messages.
screens.callout: The sender owns the final message.

screens.title: Module 6 review: multimodal creation
screens.lead: Text, images, audio, video, and documents each need quality and rights checks.

screens.title: Module 7 review: research
screens.lead: AI can guide research, but original evidence supports the claim.
bullets: Ask a clear, scoped question.
Move up the source ladder.
Open and read every important source.
Link claims to evidence.
State limits and disagreement.
screens.callout: A citation that has not been checked is not reliable evidence.

screens.title: Module 8 review: data
screens.lead: Prepare and verify data before using it for a decision.
bullets: Define rows, fields, units, and dates.

Use honest chart scales.
Separate facts, meaning, advice, and uncertainty.
screens.callout: The chart and the table must tell the same truth.

screens.title: Module 9 review: meetings
screens.lead: A meeting creates value through clear decisions and completed actions.
bullets: Start with a result and agenda.
Record only with required consent.
Separate discussion, decisions, and questions.
Give actions an owner and due point.
Verify, share safely, and follow up.
screens.callout: If nobody owns the next step, it is not a complete action item.

screens.title: Module 10 review: business adoption
screens.lead: A sound AI initiative solves a measured problem through a limited test.
bullets: Map the real process.
Set a baseline.
Bound the pilot and write stop rules.
